This review originally appeared on my blog, Books Without Any Pictures: http://bookswithoutanypictures.com/20... All Systems Red is the first book in the series The Murderbot Diaries. And really, the word murderbot is what made me pick up this book. It just *sounds* like the kind of thing I’d want to read. Luckily, my instinct was correct, and All Systems Red did not disappoint. The story is set in outer space. Space exploration is regulated by corporations, and those corporations are cheap and want to cut as many corners as possible so they can make lots and lots of money. When a group of explorers goes on a mission, the corporation makes them rent a SecUnit (security unit), an android made partially with cloned human parts, in order to protect (but mostly spy on and collect data from) the explorers. The main character of this story is a SecUnit that’s hacked its governor module and gone rogue. It doesn’t want the humans to find out, because then it would be taken apart for scrap or would have another governor module installed, and that would mean the end of its freedom. Really, Murderbot (that’s what it calls itself in private) just wants to spend some quality time watching the many many many hours of soap operas that it downloaded. The thought of socializing with humans, who both fear and pity it, isn’t at all appealing. But of course, life isn’t that easy. Someone is sabotaging the mission, and if the humans are going to survive, they’re going to have to work together with the newly rogue Murderbot to do so. I really liked the way that Murderbot is characterized throughout the story, because the author makes it very clear that even though Murderbot thinks like a person and has emotions, it isn’t a human at all. Murderbot has no gender, because it wasn’t built with any sexual parts or characteristics. It doesn’t hold grudges against the corporation or humans in general, because holding grudges is a very human thing to do. True, it has many human feelings and characteristics, but it’s also very much a robot. It doesn’t feel comfortable interacting with humans because humans either treat it with revulsion or try to humanize it, and the latter is extremely awkward for everyone involved precisely because it isn’t human. Murderbot is its own thing and doesn’t fit neatly into any of the boxes you try to put it in. It’s an alien consciousness that wasn’t supposed to happen, and now it’s trying to figure out its place in the world. I’m looking forward to the rest of this series. All Systems Red was a grand adventure, and I can’t wait to see what Murderbot will do with itself next. 1 like

Witty, playful, fast-paced, and accessible, Martha Wells' All Systems Red drops the reader into the pov of a self-described Murderbot -- a science-fictional amalgam of cloned biological human biology fused with technology and software. Before the action breaks, our Murderbot has already unlugged him/it/herself from his governor module -- going rogue leading not to genocidal rampage but rather binge-watching entertainment serials from the future net and ponderously aiming for anonymity shying away from his human crew. Assigned as a security detail with a group of planetary surveyors prior to terraforming claims, the plot quickly reveals our Murderbot to exhibit an endearing pluck and self-deprecating humanity. This novella is swift-moving, pulpy, and taut. It does not overreach nor does it underdeliver. The language and sentence balance is refreshingly competent and entertaining, as is the manner of revealing aspects of the universe, politics, and characters. Martha Wells is a talented, productive, and effective writer based on this book. If there is one drawback, it is that the diverse crew of this mission are so sparsely identified in the early going that it is a bit overwhelming. Had I tried to differentiate all the different names, it would have slowed me down. Instinctively, I just accepted them as gray noise and let the names reveal the relevant aspects of personality as the plot progressed. This is not a character piece, nor is it devoid of character. There is heart here. Thanks to my friend Alexandra for recommending this book, the first in a series. The cover of my library copy credits the book as a Hugo and Nebula Award winner, and I can see why. The accolades are deserved.

Is it strange that a novella about an anxious, misanthropic android is comfort reading? (Murderbot is not really an android, but that comes closest to what they are.) I've been reading a lot of horror and dark fiction lately, completely on purpose, but I realized I needed a bit of a break. Enter Murderbot. This series has gotten tons of good press in the sci-fi world, and if you read that stuff you have probably heard of it. If you have not, here's the elevator pitch. A security android (sorta) hacks itself so as to no longer be under the control of the company that owns it. Instead of waging war on those who have done it wrong, it decides to continue doing its job, at least half-assedly, and watch a bunch of shows. This is going pretty well, until the group it's contracted to provided security for is sabotaged and Murderbot has to save them. While doing this, it discovers it kinda likes these particular humans, and would like them to not die. The best thing about this re-read, for me, is comparing this Murderbot with the Murderbot of later books. Murderbot remains anxious and grouchy, but it's so, so much worse in this book. Murderbot is still used to hiding behind an opaque helmet, so having to talk to people face to face is deeply uncomfortable for it. At one point, it has to go face the wall to have a conversation. Another thing that's great is watching Murderbot improve at its job. It's a security expert, but it says many times that the company only cares about its clients to the extent that it would have to pay insurance on them. The company is also incredibly cheap, and Murderbot often comes up with ideas based more on the shows it watches than the actual training it has had downloaded to it. (Also, I hope no one finds me calling Murderbot 'it' upsetting. Murderbot has no gender or sexual orientation, and, at least at this point, doesn't really think of itself as a person. There's probably a good case to made for using 'they' pronouns for Murderbot, but I don't think that actually happens in the story. The story is in first person, and most people that Murderbot meets either believe it to be a thing, or they call it some alias it has picked.) Anyway, read these books, y'all. Review posted on Fantasy Literature: The narrator of All Systems Red is a once-nameless cyborg security unit or SecUnit that has given itself the name Murderbot (for reasons disclosed midway through the story). Using its own unprecedented and highly unauthorized initiative, Murderbot has hacked the governor module software that controls its actions and obligates it to be obedient. But instead of going on a killing spree, as one might expect given the name it adopted, Murderbot elects to spend its spare hours watching countless hours of video entertainment and trying not to interact more than is necessary with the group of eight humans that it’s responsible for protecting, a survey group of eight scientists called PreservationAux that is exploring the natural resources on an uninhabited planet. Murderbot’s self-isolation and studied lack of caring starts to break down, however, when potentially deadly accidents start to occur with suspicious regularity. Dr. Bharadwaj is almost killed by an alien creature that explodes out of the bottom of one of the many craters along the coast, and the group finds that data has been deleted from the warnings and fauna sections of their planetary survey package. The autopilot of their “hopper” aircraft cuts out without warning, which could have led to a fatal crash. And then there are the automated data updates that Murderbot is supposed to be uploading (and would have, if it hadn’t disabled its governor module). Matters only get worse when the group decides to visit the only other survey group on the planet. Murderbot is painfully shy and vastly reluctant to get too close to the humans, and even more, to share their secrets. But it becomes clear that the group won’t survive without Murderbot’s help and active involvement. All Systems Red is a breezy, fast-paced science fiction adventure wrapped in a light mystery. There’s not nearly as much murder and mayhem as the title and Murderbot’s name might lead one to believe. Instead, All Systems Red has something serious to say about the ideas of free will and autonomy, and about the difficulties faced by introverts in day-to-day life. Murderbot tells itself that it just doesn’t care about the humans, but its excruciating shyness soon becomes clear to the other characters and to the reader. Murderbot hides its human face behind helmet with an opaque faceplate, and awkwardly withdraws from conversations that become too personal, choosing to stand facing the wall instead. Murderbot comments that it has no gender or sex-related parts; claiming that only sexbots in brothels have those. Understandably, it has an asexual personality, another unique aspect to this main character. Murderbot fast-forwards through all of the sex scenes in the serials it watches, finding them boring (“I think that even if I did have sex-related parts I would find them boring”). You get how this could make her disinterested in the lives of her charges, so we're good. My initial impression of Murderbot is that of a teenage girl forced to attend some sort of family outing--irritated that the adult is forcing her to do some chore. As her character expands we get that it's more similar to a 2 year old being put in charge of an adult scientist and ordering them to scrap a complex experiment in favor of spraying the wall with a water gun. It isn't petulance as much as exacerbation at being forced to follow the commands of beings who aren't capable of processing data the way that she is, and those same individuals in charge often make the wrong decision, leading to her cleaning up a mess. Once again, a babysitter with guns in her arms. This leads to the major action points of the book, which is the discovery that the information they have about the world, and that there might be more than simple scientific teams exploring the area. We get a glimpse of how Murderbot is typically treated by her human contracts, in her indifference to actually learn anything about them or to be invested in anything other than doing the bare minimum to keep them alive. Befriedigend! In diesem Zusammenhang: Ich lese sonst nicht gerne SciFi-Technobabble. Oft steht er in Verbindung mit langen Beschreibungen von technischen Geräten oder astronomisch-physikalischen Erklärungen, die mich einfach nicht interessieren. In dieser Buchreihe ist der Technobabble eher im IT-Bereich angesiedelt und auch da reicht ein halbwegs oberflächliches Verständnis davon, wie ein Code oder ein Netzwerk grundsätzlich funktionieren, um folgen zu können. Ich bin Historikerin, nicht ITlerin – wenn ich das schaffe, schafft ihr das auch! Ich habe dank der Murderbot-Reihe zum ersten Mal verstanden, warum Leute sowas gerne lesen. Ich liebe es, dass das Aussehen der Personen recht spärlich beschrieben wird. Selbst von unserer Hauptfigur SecUnit erfahren wir im Verlauf der Bände nur vage Informationen zum Äußeren, abseits von „in langen Klamotten siehts wie ein Mensch mit Dataport im Nacken aus“. Das gelingt in anderen Büchern nicht so gut, aber hier werden die Figuren über ihr Verhalten, ihre Art zu sprechen und ihre Beziehungen untereinander so gut charakterisiert, dass das Aussehen so weit in den Hintergrund tritt, dass es tatsächlich so egal ist, wie es sein sollte. Davon abgesehen lese ich ohnehin nicht gern lange Beschreibungen vom Aussehen, weil ich insbesondere Frisuren und Klamotten auch einfach nicht sehr interessant finde. Urban Fantasy und Romance sind voll von solchen Beschreibungen und es könnte mir nicht egaler sein, welche Jeans die Figur heute trägt. Die Murderbot-Diaries entlasten hier meinen Arbeitsspeicher beim Lesen, indem das beschrieben wird, was ich wissen will. Und nicht das, was die Autorin oder der Autor meinen, mir unbedingt vermitteln zu müssen, damit ich mir alles richtig™ vorstelle. Naja und dann sind die gesellschaftlichen und sozialen Verhältnisse angenehm und unaufdringlich dargestellt. Verschiedene romantische Beziehungen der Menschen gehören zu deren Hintergründen, werden aber nicht tiefer thematisiert oder als Besonderheit herausgestellt. Das verleiht ihnen gebührende Selbstverständlichkeit und lässt – wieder – Platz für weitere, interessante Aspekte. Ok, wir wissen, dass Dr. Mensah zwei Ehepartner*innen und einige Kinder zuhause hat. Das ist cool – aber ist nicht ihr einziger definierender Faktor, denn rein zufällig ist sie außerdem politische Entität, wissenschaftliche Fachfrau und eine energische Anführerin. Und nicht frei von Fehlern. Insbesondere konzentriert sich die ganze Buchreihe - neben der formidablen Action - auf die Frage, wer SecUnit ist und was es will vom Leben. Loads of fun, in large part due to the main character/narrator of Murderbot. That isn't actually Murderbot's name, but it's what our narrator chooses as a self-referential, and to tell you why would possibly tell you too much about this novella. Murderbot is a Security Unit, a half-machine half-organic being created solely to protect humans in a highly corporatized, planet-faring future. The plot itself is a somewhat straightforward adventure narrative laced with progressive sci-fi concepts. The military bits occasionally get elided enough for even me, the civilian, to notice, but any criticism is quickly subsumed by how awesome Murderbot is. And that's not to imply that Murderbot is some kind of hardcore badass (tho there are definitely moments of that): on the contrary, Murderbot's appeal comes largely from the flaws of this fascinating, self-aware being as Murderbot guides and protects a group of explorers on a dangerous planet. Murderbot, you see, is the epitome of socially hostile ("antisocial" and "socially awkward" just don't accurately describe the condition.) Murderbot would much rather sit in a Cubicle, watching entertainment feeds, than interact with humans. When circumstances force Murderbot into very personal quarters with the human members of the expedition, the results are both comic and almost painfully insightful into what it means to shun human company. Any introvert can empathize. I also really enjoyed the economy of emotion put into that ending, and am very much looking forward to the rest of the novellas in the series, tho I rather wish they could all have been published together in one volume to begin with. When All Systems Red was published in 2017, I was deep in my literary phase, reading all the award shortlists and mostly ignoring core genre fiction. I don’t regret that period. Exposure to realist and experimental narratives broadened my tastes and outlook, filling a cultural hole I hadn’t known existed. But it also meant I skipped several key genre works, including The Murderbot Diaries. With the adaptation of the first novella now out on Apple TV, I decided to read it before watching the series. I now get why All Systems Red—about a self-aware Security Unit (SecUnit) that calls itself “Murderbot”—had fandom in a tizz. Murderbot is a fantastic character: its love of soap operas, irritation with humans who ask too many questions, and burgeoning sense of self after disabling its governor module are pure fandom catnip.* The overarching plot—Murderbot assigned to a planetary survey team on an uninhabited world where things quickly go to hell—is nothing a seasoned science fiction fan hasn’t seen before. It’s perfectly adequate for an origin story, but I can’t say I ever cared much about the survey team, aside from lead scientist Dr. Mensah. Her competence and relationship with Murderbot means I wouldn’t mind seeing her pop up again in future tales (yes, I’ll be reading them).** If the story didn’t wow me, I did enjoy Wells’ treatment of her protagonist. I was surprised to learn that Murderbot isn’t actually a robot, but a cyborg with both organic and cybernetic parts. This lets Wells dodge some of the tired “what is this human emotion you call love” clichés. Murderbot has emotions—it loves its soaps (even if it fast-forwards the sex scenes)—it just can’t stand people, which, fair enough. It’s also neat that it has a face to show those emotions. I also appreciated the well-modulated snark: Murderbot can be rude, but with a tonal flatness that makes it even funnier. “This is why I didn’t want to come. I’ve got four perfectly good humans here and I didn’t want them to get killed by whatever took out DeltFall. It’s not like I cared about them personally, but it would look bad on my record, and my record was already pretty terrible.” The one “robot” trope that Wells leans into involves the enslavement of a sentient being. Wells doesn’t push hard on this theme, not until the very end, but the survey crew’s discomfort with an entity they didn’t know had a face speaks volumes about this corporation-led society without needing ungainly exposition. Now, onto the Apple TV series.*** *You don’t need to be a science fiction fan to find Murderbot an engaging character. **I’ve now seen the series, and they do a decent job fleshing out the other members of the Preservation Alliance. Doctor Gurathin, played by the always great David Dastmalchian, almost steals the show, which surprised me given he’s a one-note character in the novella. ***Which, as I note above, I’ve now seen. It’s good. A faithful adaptation that fleshes out the ensemble cast and adds some colour to the broader Murderbot Universe. I’m happy they’ve renewed the series.

All Systems Red by Martha Wells is a novella I have heard a lot of people saying a lot of good things about. The only other book I've read by Martha Wells was kind of meh, so I'm glad the critical mass of people praising this book was well and truely exceeded for me to pick it up. It was an excellent read. All Systems Red had me from the opening paragraph which, as I immediately tweeted, was a delight. It's told in first person from the point of view of a cyborg. A bored cyborg who has gained free will and really just wants to watch TV between half-arsing its contractual duties enough to hide its illegal free will. Unfortunately, the survey mission that should have been straightforward and relatively dull — from Murderbot's point of view, if not the scientists it's protecting — turns out to be anything but. This novella was brief but excellent. It had mystery, danger, adventure, a compelling voice and made me laugh many times. It was also an interesting look at humanity and where the lines are drawn. Murderbot counts as machinery rather than as human because of how it was constructed. But it still feels emotions and has independent thoughts and we get the impression that even if it hadn't given itself free will it would still be having these thoughts and feelings, it just wouldn't be able to act on them. On the one hand considered non-human, on the other sentient and enslaved. And we see augmented humans who have some similarities with Murderbots in terms of data processing and telemetry (for lack of a better word) but are definitely human. I assume these are themes that will be explored further in the sequel novellas. All Systems Red was an excellent read and I recommend it to all fans of speculative fiction. It's a quick read and you don't even have to like robots or military SF to enjoy it. I cannot wait until the next novella comes out. “I could have become a mass murderer after I hacked my governor module, but then I realized I could access the combined feed of entertainment channels carried on the company satellites. It had been well over 35,000 hours or so since then, with still not much murdering, but probably, I don’t know, a little under 35,000 hours of movies, serials, books, plays, and music consumed. Having said that, The Murderbot Diaries have been on my radar for years, so when I realised All Systems Red fit the prompt for a reading challenge the choice was easy. All Systems Red is the first in the series of novellas by Martha Wells (that will number 8 when Platform Decay is released in May 2026) introducing a hybrid organic android who calls itself Murderbot. Owned by The Company, Murderbot is one of dozens of ‘SecUnits’, deployed to protect people or property, or kill and destroy the same, as management decrees. Murderbot however, is different. After a system malfunction that resulted in the unsanctioned slaughter of fifty seven clients, Murderbot (who adopted the name as a result), hacked their own system, and secretly severed The Company’s control. As the story opens, Murderbot, who keeps up the pretence of their programming lest The Company order their destruction, is accompanying a small group of non-profit scientists assessing the value of a planet’s resources. The mission is entirely uneventful until suddenly it’s not, and Murderbot is pulling a scientist from the mouth of a tunnelling carnivorous monster, sparring with a batch of hijacked SecUnits, faking out unscrupulous rival surveyors, and having to spend way too much time with humans when they’d much rather be watching Sanctuary Moon. Cynical and stoic yet awkward and vulnerable, Murderbot has a surprisingly complexity. I enjoyed how the dynamic between Murderbot and the group of humans under his protection further informed his character. Despite the brevity of the novella format, Wells raises questions about identity, autonomy, and humanity, all with a delightfully deadpan sense of humour. I've been looking forward to reading this novella since the preview chapter went up on Tor.com, and let me tell you, I was not disappointed. The initial draw for me was the protagonist. Wells does an amazing job of sketching out Murderbot's core concept in a the few few paragraphs: security droid who is secretly self-aware but would rather watch soap operas than go on a murderous rampage. She also does an amazing job with Murderbot's voice, giving it life an personality as it makes its own (not terribly flattering) observations of the humans its charged with guarding. Wells is really careful to capture and leave out the things that Murderbot would and wouldn't care about, which gives its voice a very distinct flavor since its priorities are obviously different. It's an interesting take on "machine becomes self-aware"; Murderbot doesn't think about things in a human way, but also not in a mechanical way. There's so much personality in Murderbot that I actually wonder how self-aware bots are when they don't have cracked governors. It's a rather terrible thought. Beneath the flippancy of Murderbot's voice, though, there is the subplot of Murderbot trying to figure out what to do now that it is self-aware. Honestly, avoiding the whole question with a 400+ episode soap opera sounds like a pretty good way to go about things. The way Murderbot describes its interactions with the humans its guarding is especially fascinating, due to the contrast with how Murderbot tosses off descriptions versus what the reader's reconstruction of the scene and awareness of how strange things like abruptly walking away to stare at a corner rather than people would be to the humans around it. Mild spoilers for "All Systems Red" follow. Wells uses Murderbot's discomfort with attention, assertion, and being treated as a free agent to pull off a narrative trick that I didn't figure out until the very end. The story is written in 1st person past, but at the very end Murderbot's voice switches abruptly to directly addressing the reader. The whole novella is reframed as a personal message to another of the characters. So Murderbot's been talking about the other characters in 3rd person the entire time while they've been reading about themselves being viewed in 3rd person the whole time. It's a surprising jolt but it makes SO MUCH sense that in trying to explain its very personal motivations for leaving Dr. Mensah and the team, Murderbot would start from a very remote place -- and only at the very end change, when it didn't have any choice, close that distance. It's SO good and so cleverly done. Spoilers end. In addition to all of this, the plot is an excellent intrigue adventure and really clips along. The novella totally flew by me; I read it twice in a row and loved it. So highly recommended for those in search of a sci-fi adventure with some really clever writing and entertaining voice work. I'm really looking forward to the next novella in the series.

I really enjoyed 'All Systems Red' by Martha Wells. The story of a part organic, part robotic security unit, or SecUnit, tasked with looking after a small group of scientists and technicians on an expedition to another planet. It's told from the point of view of the SecUnit, who, after secretly hacking and disabling the governor module that controls its behaviour and obedience, now refers to itself (if only in private) as Murderbot, and is painfully shy and would rather be watching the serials they've downloaded from the entertainment feeds, mostly of a show called 'Rise And Fall Of Sanctuary Moon', than interact with people. But when suspicious things start happening, as well as another research station suddenly going off line, SecUnit reluctantly has to get involved with the expedition group to find out what is happening and is surprised to find that they want to protect 'their humans'. Its a fast paced and enjoyable read, a mix of science fiction and thrilling mystery. I liked the setting up of the corporate funded expeditions and the world building that surrounded it. I got vibes of Duncan Jones' 'Moon' movie with a big conglomo that only cares about profit and does things on the cheap. The character of SecUnit was really well fleshed out and I liked the personality that came through slowly as the bot came to terms of having to interact with the group of researchers it was there to protect, becoming more human than robot. Although it's written as an androgynous cyborg, I had the impression of it being female for some reason. Dr Mensah, the lead on the expedition, and the rest of the scientists and technicians came across as likeable and were a well knit team, even Dr Gurathin, who was suspicious of the SecUnit. Each had their own personalities and concerns, making them seem like a real group of people rather than just a bunch of generic scientists on an expedition. The only downside for me is that it was over too quickly, as I was really enjoying the novella, but as it's the first in a series of four stories, the next being 'Artificial Condition', which is now available (as of May 2018), I will definitely be looking forward to reading more of the Murderbot Diaries. science-fiction

“SecUnit would like to file a formal complaint: too many feelings, not enough media streaming.” All Systems Red by Martha Wells came out in 2017 and kicks off The Murderbot Diaries with a pretty perfect balance of bite, boredom, and barely-contained chaos. The plot is simple enough. A security android has hacked its own governor system and is technically free but still stuck guarding a crew of humans on a survey mission. It would rather be doing literally anything else. Mostly watching media feeds and being left alone. But then corporate sabotage, mystery threats, and of course… feelings get in the way. The world is gritty without being overloaded with sci-fi jargon. The stakes are real. And the whole thing wraps up in a clean, tight novella that somehow manages to feel like a full story without overstaying its welcome. Murderbot is what makes it all work. That voice is weirdly relatable. Sarcastic, tired, often annoyed but still deeply competent. The way it reacts to people, stress, and even kindness feels believable, and more than a few scenes made me laugh out loud. The pacing never lags. It flies forward with a kind of breathless efficiency, but never feels rushed or empty. The plot knows what it wants to do and does it. There’s no filler. It felt kind of refreshing to read something that knew exactly how long it needed to be and didn’t try to puff itself up. Honestly, I could’ve read another 100 pages of Murderbot just hating everything and I wouldn’t have been mad. Solid 4/5.

review_text: Totally unexpected and refreshing. Really quite excellent, actually. It would've rated higher, but it was short and left me wanting more whereas a 5-star book leaves me feeling sated. Based on the title I thought this was going to be a violent SF horror novel, but it's misleading. A cyborg SecUnit who thinks of himself as "Murderbot" is rented out as security detail to a team of human scientists doing planetary research. Unlike millions of other SecUnits, this one is complicated, smart and individualistic - things that Units aren't supposed to be. As the situation on the planet becomes dangerous and the SecUnit shows himself to be trustworthy, his clients grow attached to him. And although he's programmed to be impersonal, he grows fond of them in a distant, confused way. The best part of this book is seeing how the SecUnit fights against emotions he doesn't understand and doesn't want to understand. Although I enjoyed the skulduggery elements too (I have thus far neglected to mention the major storyline involving sabotage, murder and bribery), it was the brilliantly written SecUnit's struggle with his unnatural feelings of humanity that pushed this book from good to great and nearly perfect. At just over a 150 paged this book is all killer no filler telling the story of Murderbot, a recently self aware half organic/robotic, who at the start of the story has recently hacked his system so that he is beholden to nobody and can do as he pleases. The book covers a research team on a remote planet who are there for preservation and the Murderbot is supplied by the company who allow such expeditions as protection to this crew. What follows is a thrilling tale of murder, a rival faction seeking to get the resources this planet has and to eliminate anyone else who are there. Murderbot is the first person narrator of this book and his new found freedom leads to some funny and witting internal monologue as he tries to cope and deal with his humans who he no longer is obligated to protect but does so anyway because he likes their leader. The book as plenty of action and the resolution is true to the Murderbot’s character especially since you spend the whole book in his head, as he reflects on what he wants based on his newfound feelings and the media feed which he obsessively watches throughout the novel which are also a source of some of the funnier moments. 4.5 stars This did really well what it set out to do and I immensely enjoyed it. Not a breath-taking work of fiction, not a masterpiece passed down through generations, but really good, really fun, original, creative, interesting, and most importantly genuine. This murderbot has a heart because this novella has a heart. And the other way around. What am I? Who am I? What am I supposed to be doing on this planet? Those are questions that our protagonist has to face and doesn't really have an answer for. And yet their (its?) struggle felt almost like an answer to those same question running through the reader's own head. If not even the murderbot needs a purpose for existing or should be tied down by strict rules and duties... why should I? why should we? Please don't misunderstand though, this novel is not heavily philosophic. It's actually rather fast paced and action packed, all things considered. I've talked about how the name "Murderbot" made me roll my eyes a few times already on my blog, but I've got to reiterate that point: it really, really sounds corny. I'm glad I managed to get past the name, though, because beneath that corniness is a story that actually really worked for me. Following the internal monologue of the self-proclaimed Murderbot, All Systems Red tells a story of social anxiety and learning how to function in a world where you feel like an outsider. It's a really great read, and the internal deliberations of the Murderbot are the highlight here, but even that's supported extremely well with an intriguing sci-fi mystery plot. The survey team who employ the SecUnit are all interesting characters in their own right, even if they weren't given much time to grow and develop. I liked them and I hope they show up again in later installments in this series. As for the story, it's nothing new and was pretty predictable, but it has plenty of mysterious data breaches and questionable corporate motivations to interest most sci-fi fans. All Systems Red is a short read, clocking in at about 150 pages, so you'll likely be able to finish it up in about a day. All Systems Red has a distinct plot and likeable secondary characters, but for me its main failing is the protagonist Murderbot. Murderbot's narration is juvenile. Wells hardly provides any information about why Units are manufactured the way--part organic, part robotic--and my question at the end was, why bother with the expensive organic parts and consciousness that needs to be overridden by modules when it would be objectively cheaper to use robots? As the only substantially developed science fiction element of the story, I wanted a lot more information. How did it became ubiquitous to manufacture and use these entities with the potential for free will? Potentially a question that will be explored in the sequels, but not one I will stick around to find out the answer to. Murderbot's main traits are being conflicted about its identity as half organic/half mechanical, and watching a lot of television. Specifically, over 35,000 hours or close to four years since it hacked its government module...yet it has a startling lack of identity for a unit that sought, and has had, autonomy for that long. Additionally, no basis of comparison for previous missions was provided. Although it's implied that this is the first time the humans have considered Murderbot to be a person, I wanted it to be more clear about what had changed with this mission. At 150 pages, All Systems Red didn't have space to provide background that would have helped me be more invested. The plot works! But I also didn't find myself surprised by anything that happened -- the antagonists are predictable and quickly dealt with, and there are no real consequences for the crew. And then, a small pet peeve of mine: Murderbot is nearly killed/off-lined multiple times...for such a short book, that's way too much almost dying. The emotional resonance wore off. I can absolutely see the appeal of this novel for some, but it wasn't for me. 8 likes 1 comment

The introduction to The Murderbot Diaries is simply great fun! A refreshing and diverting sci-fi novella with wide appeal; a marvellous package of wry humour, suspense and a healthy dose of compassion. As much as I love science fiction, I don't consider myself as a hardcore reader of the genre, and there are a lot of popular series or "required reading" which I have yet to catch-up on. In this respect, I find this book to be original; it is not a space opera, cyberpunk and it is not about an alien invasion. This is a first-person perspective narrative of a humanlike bot, a construct of both organic and inorganic parts, who finds it/him/herself becoming weird and messed up with increasing ‘emotions' while dealing with her human clients even though the bots are not programmed as such. (Okay, I am going to call the bot a ‘her' because even though it is technically genderless, I can't help picturing it as a female. The voice of her first-person perspective just sounds feminine, in my opinion). Check out its hook right at the beginning. I could have become a mass murderer after I hacked my governor module, but then I realised I could access the combined feed of entertainment feed carried on the company satellites. It had been well over 35,000 hours or so since then, with still not much murdering, but probably, I don't know, a little under 35,000 hours of movies, serials, books, plays, and music consumed. As a heartless killing machine, I was a terrible failure. Now, tell me that you don't want to keep on reading after that! The Murderbot (a self-proclaimed name) is an introverted, socially awkward/anxious ‘geek' who couldn't wait to get back to her serials once her job is done instead of hanging around with her human clients to whom she was contracted to as the SecUnit. In corporate-dominated space travel, this was the order of the day for all entities who want to conduct explorations or surveys on various planets. One SecUnit for every ten humans for security reasons, the contractee will also be using the company's habitats, database and communications systems, and an emergency beacon. As the contracts are, strangely, won by the lowest bidder, the company is cheap and we get a lot of humourous narrative about the deplorable quality and condition of the company's software and hardware from the Murderbot's point-of-view. Even as a construct, the Murderbot is completely relatable and endearing, especially the way she keeps wanting to go back to her serials or trying to sneak in some time to watch her entertainment feeds. There are too many times when I feel a desperate need to be left alone to my books; a feeling I am sure every avid reader out there shares one way or another. While I can't call myself a social misfit, this is something I empathise with, where any form of interaction can be absolutely frightening, particularly when it involves eye contact and physical touch. The underlying message of the story goes down deeper into the theme of slavery and social outcasts, which these bots essentially are in respect to the humans. The story is most compelling and amusing when she finds herself feeling out of sorts with her current client, a bunch of scientists and explorers whom she found herself liking, and much to her chagrin were intent on treating her as one of them. Her observation of this group was a hilarious analogy to her serials. The whole group had been remarkably drama-free so far, which I appreciated. The last few contracts had been like being an involuntary bystander in one of the entertainment feed's multi-partner relationship serials except I'd hated the whole cast. There are plenty more of such amusing asides as she and her clients found themselves in a life or death situation. As a rogue SecUnit with a hacked governor module who liked her clients enough not to see them killed, she endeavoured to save them from whatever or whoever is trying to hunt them down. There are great moments of suspense from this arc, although I did find its ending to be quite abrupt. With its crisp and captivating delivery in a morsel-sized story, I am looking forward to more adventures with the Murderbot. ‘All Systems Red’ by Martha Wells is the first of what will be called the Murderbot Diaries. The narrator is a snarky robot who speaks like a witty teenager. Xe (it does not have a sex, so using s/he pronouns are erroneous, so, I will use Xe) is a security bot or SecUnit. Xe works for a commercial company responsible for setting up transportation, habitat construction and security for other private for-profit companies or humanitarian or scientific non-profits who wish to explore other planets occupied by non-sentient life forms or simply planetary objects which have important minerals which can be monetized. Xe calls itself Murderbot because its programming involves killing anything which threatens the people who have contracted with the Company for exploration services. However, the Company and everybody else does not know Murderbot hacked its own governor module after a previous protection assignment went wrong. Xe has been autonomous ever since. As the novella opens, Xe is protecting a non-profit group of scientists exploring a planet full of non-sentient life. Xe thinks they seem nice, but humans do not really interest Xe beyond paying attention if they ask it. Mostly Xe watches downloads of soap operas while scanning the area for trouble periodically. Xe’s humans are busy exploring a crater when stuff begins to happen which require Xe's services - very bad, life-threatening stuff, the kind of trouble which looks like someone or something is trying to kill all of the scientists! The scientists are scared and so is Xe! What is going on? It is possible from clues that Murderbot's owners, the Company, could be part of whatever is happening. Something issued a command to Xe, trying to take control. No one knows Xe hacked the governor module, so Xe is on its own. As far as Xe is concerned, no one is going to harm the human scientists! Xe sort of likes them. So do I, gentle reader. I highly recommend this novella. It is a really fun adventure, well written, and very entertaining. It also is sneakily exploring situations in which people and sentient, but enslaved, robots might find themselves interacting. Xe felt female to me, but maybe you will see Xe differently. This novella's strengths are its relentless pace and its unique main character. Murderbot is a non-binary half bot / half human construct, that is painfully shy and is still figuring out its own personality, while initially trying to pretend that it is just a SecUnit that is following orders. Turns out its humans are really nice, though, which only makes matters worse, because now there might be other reasons to actually try to keep them alive, apart from it looking bad on Murderbot's record if it fails to do so. Murderbot, however, feels far more comfortable with the fictional characters of its favorite soap opera than it does with being around real people. While the awkward interactions between Murderbot and the rest of the crew are rather sweet, the rogue SecUnit's inner monologue is often extremely funny. It is snarky, a little grumpy, sarcastic. Well written AI influenced sci fi. (My score reflects that I am not a great fan of sci fi, but it has won many awards when originally published in 2017, and I can see why - it is an enjoyable set up and set of characters, and with a relatively simple plot). The story is told by the Murderbot, who is a constructed AI robot with some organic (human-style) bits and is owned by a company that leases it out to provide security for companies (in this case exploring new planets for valuable minerals). The bot gets direct downloads of various kinds, and is equipped with weapons. Murderbots are much harder to kill than humans (for one thing they are encased in armour), and most parts of them can be replaced by the company – or if things go wrong they can be scrapped. This Murderbot is uncomfortable about interaction with humans, but is skilled at interpreting their emotions and actions. It prefers to have time in a separate part of the space unit, and when in human company to keep its face shield opaque (though the head part is installed to not frighten them being a ‘standard, generic human’ head p15). However it has a form of intelligence that has allowed it to subvert some of the things built into the AI by the company. In particular it has dismantled the governor unit that allows it to be directly controlled by the company, but also has done that in a way where their own systems will not pick it up. So in that sense it has agency – freedom to act by its own control. It also seems to experience interests and boredom, and specializes in downloading entertainment soapie type programs and spending a lot of time watching them, and on the other hand, ignoring downloads and security updates and only taking up what it sees as relevant. Many reviewers have commented positively on the engaging character and voice of this Murderbot – it doesn’t have a sex, but I can imagine it being played by a lugubrious older British actor. The set up emphasizes a number of things about the context – in particular the ongoing profit motive driving things, and the way in which the company does things in the cheapest way that seems viable, so things can go wrong because of the ‘crap’ materials. It also sets out three categories of beings in a class type of hierarchy: humans, cyber enhanced humans, and murderbots. It is common for the murderbots to be seen and treated as robots, but in this story the team, especially the leader Mensah, begin to see the bot as having an identity, and caring for it. Similarly, the bot begins to act to save and ‘care for’ the humans, beyond what has been apparently built in. The central plot is about some of the info systems and energy beginning to not be available, and the bot and crew suspecting the crew of the unit they were about to hook up with and reload from has been attacked and killed. They do find most of the crew dead, with some robots having apparently gone rogue (actually reprogrammed by some others I think), and Murderbot and the human crew perform various actions to save each other at different points. As a result when they get back to the company control, Mensah arranges to permanently buy the Murderbot so they can ‘adopt it’. In this context this is seen somewhat like buying and liberating a slave. But Murderbot doesn’t want to exchange one type of surveillance and control for another (albeit one partly based on empathy and care) and the story finishes with it managing to disable ways it can be traced and hitch-hiking a ride somewhere else where no-one knows of its existence.

The difficulty of reconciling one’s private self with one’s public façade produces a multitude of anxieties that manifest in different ways. For the self-styled Murderbot of Martha Wells "All Systems Red", a SecUnit (security robot) who lacks the full autonomy the privileged class (in this case, humans) enjoy, the coveting of its private self is not just a way to stay sane, but a way to remain alive and employed. Its internal monologue expresses a deep cynicism and flippant attitude toward its human employers – an emotional defense mechanism if ever there was one – even as it admits to itself that it likes most of the humans it is trying to avoid connecting with. From the start we are told that Murderbot has hacked its “governor” – a deeply flawed piece of regulatory software that ensures its adherence to protocol – and could conceivably go on an indiscriminate murder spree whenever it wants. It doesn’t, though, because like most of us it just wants to watch tv serials and not be hunted down and destroyed by angry humans who don’t want to be murdered. So Murderbot performs its duties protecting the scientific survey team it was assigned to, faithful to the programming it doesn’t technically have to adhere to anymore in order to jealously guard its secret self – until protecting the team and keeping its secret become incompatible. Lest you think this is just a cerebral character study about living with double consciousness, let me assure you that it is mostly made up of robot battles and bullets shredding things and shit blowing up – its thinkiness is an important complimentary component of the whole, but far from the whole itself. In other words, "All Systems Red" is the best kind of science fiction. Murderbot’s character arc – a journey from insular self-awareness to true self-knowledge – is the story’s heart, and its most entertaining feature as well. 59 likes 6 comments

I'm not sure if I should be worried when one of the most relatable protagonists I've read in a long time is technically a robot... Being set in an unknown future on some far off planet, this book follows a security robot that managed to hack itself. The premise is simple, yet effective, and we end up with an interesting protagonist who we follow very closely. Despite its relatively short length, this book does a great job of building up and even developing the main character who embodies certain qualities I suspect resonate with most people (even if a fair few wouldn't like to admit the fact). Who wouldn't rather be relaxing in bed and watching serials instead of doing their job and interacting with people? :P The world is also surprisingly well developed for such a short story. It cleverly limits its focus to the immediate setting and only gives us information relevant to the plot. After having read quite a few long-winded fantasy and sci-fi books recently, this was a nice change. I especially enjoyed the tidbits we get about 'the company', with its unfortunately too familiar profit-centric approach to everything they do. The writing wasn't too bad either. The story was well structured, albeit with the consequence of being a tad simple and predictable. Most of the interactions between characters were well done and even though I thought there was a bit too much internal monologuing, I mostly enjoyed hearing the protagonist's thoughts. We ended up with quite a few questions remaining though, so I got a sense of incompleteness to the story, although that might be due to this being a series. I would have liked to know more about their motivations, but again, being so short, I understand why it was so limited. So there you have it. My biggest problem is the characters - And there are quite a few of them. The sad thing is, that I cant even tell you how many characters there are. I estimate that there are 6 - 10 characters in the book, but they are all so bland and frankly non-essential to the plot, that I could not tell them apart. You get little to no information about them other than a name and a team function. There are also some interpersonal relations between them, but again they do not matter for the plot at all. The plot itself is thin, and only works if you care about the characters, and since I didn't, the plot did not work for me at all. The world building is basically non-existent. Lots of references to other places and cultures, but no info on them. Its basically just all footnotes. I am not usually this harsh in my reviews, and always try to give the book the benefit of the doubt, but in this case I simply don't think this book is worth your time. 3.25 stars I read the first three books in the Murderbot series - All Systems Red, Artificial Condition, and Rogue Protocol. I'm reviewing them together since I have similar feelings about each of these books. I'm not generally a sci-fi reader, but I've heard good things about this series from a number of different sources, and I do like expanding my reading horizons. I decided to listen to the first three books since together they are about the length of a regular novel. Murderbot is a SecUnit, aka a Security Unit, aka a killing machine. SecUnits are bots with some organic features that make them appear mostly (or at least partially) human. They exist in a future highly capitalistic society where companies sell rights to planetary research and development. Murderbot is rented out as a required part of packages granting rights, and his job is to protect his team at all costs, which often involves the murder of any threats. Murderbot, however, is different. He's been able to disconnect his governor module, which previously required him to obey orders, and act autonomously, although this is a fact he's trying to conceal, as absolutely no one would be okay with a rogue SecUnit. Rather than doing his job, he basically just wants to spend hours watching the future version of Netflix - very relatable! Yet despite his urge to tune out, Murderbot finds that he actually does care. In each of the first three volumes he finds himself in situations where he takes an active role in protecting a group of humans. He's also interested in investigating an incident from his past that caused him to give himself the nickname Murderbot (this is an ongoing storyline throughout the first three volumes in the series). The series starts in media res, with us jumping into the action and slowly getting pieces of information that help us make sense of the world. While I appreciate not having to wade through pages and pages of worldbuilding (as is sometimes the penchant in sci-fi novels), it also made for a slightly disorienting experience. What Murderbot is doing is pretty easy to follow, but why things are happening sometimes took a bit longer for me to wrap my head around. These books are short and super fast-paced, probably even too fast-paced. In the first book, the climax of the drama was over almost as soon as I realized what was going on. I wouldn't mind a bit more world-building and explanation and denouement. Also, in a world where so much communication happens over various feeds, Murderbot and his allies seem to be able to easily hack into any system that they need access to, but they rarely have to worry about being hacked into. That part felt a little too easy and convenient to me. I enjoyed these books and definitely see why others like them. That being said, I don't think I'll continue with the series. My curiosity has been satiated and there are many other books I want to read. review_text: Do you remember Isaac Asimov’s I, Robot? No, not the movie with Wil Smith…that basically borrowed the name but little else. The book was a collection of stories that explored humankind’s future with robots. The key robot was R. Daneel Olivaw. You may recall the three laws of Robotics: 1) A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm. 2) A robot must obey orders given to it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the First Law. 3) A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law. That only works if your robot’s implant hasn’t been hacked. Wells’ robot is good at hacking and has a few deaths in its past. It refers to itself as “Murderbot” but doesn’t share this with the group of humans who it is now responsible for. It is a far cry from R. Daneel Olivaw, but that's part of what makes this "diary" so interesting. Our team is on an unexplored planet trying to get to know the geology, geography, flora and fauna. Right off the bat, one of the “fauna” almost kills a member of the crew and our ‘bot barely saves him. The crew is appreciative but all our ‘bot wants to do is be left alone so it can hack into its favorite library of “soap operas.” This has some effect on team dynamics: “Now they knew their murderbot didn’t want to be around them any more than they wanted to be around it. I’d given a tiny piece of myself away. That can’t happen. I have too much to hide, and letting one piece go means the rest isn’t as protected.” Wells does a brilliant job of giving us the ‘bot’s perspective and this novella is the start of the series. She shows her usual deft touch with plot and characterization. It will be hard to resist jumping into the next one; particularly with such encouragement from GR friend Carol. 39 likes 7 comments

I came to this series already loving the author. The tone and character voice make this series so easy to love, and it's the same as we see in her other work. As the series title suggests, this is about a Murderbot - what the manufacturers call a SecUnit - who has managed to reconfigure its own governor module though all it really does with the freedom is enjoy trashy television. Incredibly lethal, SecUnits quite rightly cause concern in those around them... and I mean, we've all been raised on fiction where robots decide it sounds like an excellent idea to 'kill all humans', so having one around for security who is armed to the teeth and perfectly calibrated for murder? Great! Imagine how the humans would react if they found out that their security unit isn't under the control of its governance module, eh? What adds an interesting level of complexity is how human Murderbot looks, which is why it usually leaves the helmut opaque. What's also interesting is that it can feel pain and have emotions, and is mostly incredibly anxious around humans. It also carries quite a bit of distain for humans and yet also develops (or already has) quite high morals, and comes to react protectively of its humans without much time spent on the matter. At only 144 pages so much happens in this novella. Pretty quickly the team Murderbot is hired to protect find themselves in far more danger than they bargained for. There are quite a few members in the team but Murderbot is so much more interesting than all of them, expect perhaps the leader of the expedition, Dr. Mensah, who becomes somewhat important for our protagonist. All Systems Red was truly a delight. A snarky robot with a TV addiction? Who can resist that! All planetary missions must be supplied by the Company and they must rent a Company supplied SecUnit, an android security guard. The narrator of All Systems Red is one such SecUnit, but it has hacked into the governor module and is now secretly autonomous. It refers to itself as Murderbot, and it really doesn’t care about it’s job — guarding a team of scientists on a remote planet where there shouldn’t be problems anyway. Murderbot much prefers to hack into a satellite and gain access to 35,000 hours of entertainment media. This works out perfectly fine for Murderbot until a neighboring mission goes dark and their own humans may be in danger. The plot is not what’s important about All Systems Red. Instead, this science fiction novella focuses on the inner life of it’s protagonist and narrator, Murderbot. I know what you’re thinking: this is probably one of those robot stories where there’s a lot of angst and questioning about the nature of humanity. All Systems Red isn’t like that. There’s absolutely zero angst, and Murderbot finds humans awkward and slightly annoying. It says it likes fictional humans better than real humans, which is entirely relatable. Murderbot’s voice was far and away the best thing about All Systems Red. It’s hilarious! I was seriously laughing out loud while reading this. Robots with feelings are the best sort of robots, even if in this case our robot narrator is anti-social and largely apathetic. Although, Murderbot may be a bit less apathetic than it seems. While it professes to be horrified by the humans clumsy attempts to befriend it, it does seem to care about them beneath it all. As well as being astonishingly funny, it’s also quite heart warming. I loved All Systems Red so much. It will undoubtedly end up being one of the best science fiction stories I read all year. Thank goodness Martha Wells is writing a sequel! I desperately need more. This was a fine book. It was enjoyable in the moment of reading, but it also felt like it wouldn’t leave much of an impression on me. The book starts in media res of an action scene, and the author efficiently illustrates the world-building simply by letting the story play out. By the end of the first chapter you get a fun action scene and a foundational understanding of this sci-fi world and how secunits work, as well as some questions about world building that are soon answered in later chapters. The author shows instead of telling. I also noticed that chapter endings made me want to start the next chapter immediately. The pacing was good. However, I am not a fan of the quirky awkwardness of the narrator. I’m also irritated by robots always being autistic-coded in sci-fi. It makes sense in the world why the secunit wouldn’t get along with humans. But I bet there are more fictional autistic robots than there are fictional autistic humans. It’s a sensible metaphor, but it is so played out. There was a handful of horrible cliches in the writing, like in the line, “but my speed was off the charts.” I think the fact that these few instances distracted me from the rest of the quote-good writing says more about me than the author. But still that line made me want to return the book early. The issue of personhood and autonomy felt underdeveloped until the very end. And the ending surprised me in a good way. I’ll admit it made me want to read a sequel. Overall, this book didn’t really challenge me. It didn’t challenge my idea of what it means to be a person. It didn’t challenge my ideas of what are ethical practices for pioneering, settling, resource extraction. It was an entertaining novella, but I won’t be thinking about it nearly as long as I think about books that I love, and even books that I hate! For its brevity and the quality of writing, this book is worth a read.

listened on audio… YAWN LOL —————— Original Review 6/24/18: Yes, talk to Murderbot about it's feelings. The idea was so painful I dropped to 97 percent efficiency. I'm not much of a sci-fi gal, since the jargon and overall concepts usually confuse me. I also am just not really into futuristic stories or stories set in space, since I can't conceptualize a lot of whats going on. But after having some success with the Illuminae Files series, I'm intrigued by the genre. I picked up All Systems Red because it's less than 150 pages and I've seen some pretty good reviews of it, so I figured if I should start with sci-fi anywhere, it should be here. Overall, I liked this book. Murderbot is hilarious and honestly one of the most relatable characters I've come across. The trope of a self-aware AI with a sense of humor is always so funny and appealing to me, and I loved reading from its point-of-view. I think it's pretty awesome when an author can make a robot relatable. I, for some reason, got a very femme vibe from Murderbot, even though it has no gender. I've never gotten a female impression from any AI I've ever read, but there's something about this antisocial queen that tugged on my heartstrings. Maybe I just saw a bit too much of myself in Murderbot. I think one of the funniest parts of the book is when Dr. Mensah asked if Murderbot would like to spend time with the crew, and Murderbot--who cannot control its facial expressions readily--gives a look of absolute horror at the prospect of spending time with people. Like, bitch, me too. Talking to people is hard. Murderbot also stands in the corner of the room facing the wall when talking in group settings and I just wish that behavior was acceptable for me, because same. The writing is a little choppy and not very pretty, but I've never read anything else by Martha Wells, so I'm not sure if this was a tactic to make it truly seem like a robot was telling us the story or if she's just a writer who doesn't care about whether her words sound nice. I didn't hate it, but sometimes the choppy wording and sentences could be a tad awkward and I would have to reread them. But the writing lent itself to letting the story move fast, which I always like. What flopped in this book for me was the plot and the ending. The last two chapters were confusing and vague, and I couldn't tell you what the GrayCris group was trying to accomplish and why Murderbot's group had anything to do with it. It was never explained, and I found the fact that Murderbot was unconcious for a majority of the action scenes to be a tad lazy on the author's part. The last chapter was also weird, I don't understand quite what happened since it seemed like everything important had been completely missed by Murderbot and no one bothered to explain it to them. The last few pages seemed out of character for Murderbot as well, and I have no idea why it ended that way or where it will take us in the future. I know this is a series with 3 more books, so I'm guessing we'll learn a lot more about that planet they were on, their mission, the GrayCris group, and why everything happened the way it did. But it seems kind of silly to me to have a 150 page book were things sort of happened and but never got explained. I wanted to love this story, because I really love Murderbot, but nothing seemed to make much sense by the end. I will definitely continue the series since these books are so short and I want more of Murderbot's hilarious narration. September 2024: I loved this even more the second time. May 2018: I was so charmed by this little novella. People have been giving it great reviews, but I don't normally get very emotionally involved in shorter pieces of fiction. I was emotionally involved with this one after about fifteen pages. All Systems Red is the first novella of four (the rest set to be released by the end of the year) in the Murderbot Diaries series. Our narrator is Murderbot. He calls himself that ironically. In reality, he is a SecUnit, an android that is rented out by corporations, and who has hacked his own system to give himself control over his thoughts and actions. (I keep calling him "he," but really, Murderbot is gender neutral. But I can't seem to help myself.) The humans who have rented him out for their expedition have no idea that their SecUnit is rogue. Mostly because he still does everything they need him to, and only uses his freedom to watch hours and hours and hours of downloaded entertainment. Sometimes he is doing this while pretending to do something else. He particularly enjoys what seems to be a nighttime soap called Sanctuary Moon. He finds this easier than dealing with the world. I was already enjoying myself thoroughly because Murderbot is so sarcastic (sample line: "The hostile that had just exploded up out of the ground had a really big mouth, so I felt I needed a really big gun"), but I just melted all over inside when Murderbot takes off his armor and is revealed to be a human hybrid, and not a full robot, like the humans have assumed (it becomes clear that is an assumption Murderbot wants them to make, but more on that later). The specific thing that made me melt is that he was cold and had to wrap himself up in a blankie, and the contrast between a cold, robotic killing machine that you expect, and the actual living being that has feelings and likes to be warm and comfy almost made me lose my mind out of immediate and intense affection for the lonely little guy. (Again, very well may be feminine or completely androgynous, but he doesn't seem to care one way or the other. Gender seems to be something humans do, not Murderbots.) "So, I'm awkward with actual humans. It's not paranoia about my hacked governor module, and it's not them; it's me. I know I'm a horrifying murderbot, and they know it, and it makes both of us nervous, which makes me even more nervous. Also, if I'm not in the armor then it's because I'm wounded and one of my organic parts may fall off and plop on the floor at any moment and no one wants to see that." "Gurathin, I told you. It's shy." So I want to talk about what feels so fresh about this story, and that's how it upends our expectations about what types of stories are told about robots and humans existing together. I mean, I've been around the block. I've seen BSG, iRobot, etc. Robots, we're people, too! And that can be a very compelling narrative. But that's not what Wells seems to be interested in. Her protagonist is shy. He likes the humans to think of him as a thing, to forget he has organic parts. He doesn't like when they are reminded of his existence as more than a tool at their disposal. He keeps his faceplate down at all times. And when he's forced into situations in which the humans are confronted with his personhood (seeing his face unarmored, seeing him wounded, etc.) he becomes SO UNCOMFORTABLE. I am fascinated by this. And you can come at it from different ways. You could argue that Murderbot has been conditioned to see himself as a thing as well, and that he doesn't know how to be a person because no one has ever treated him like one. But what really interests me here is the burden of other people's expectations, and how much Murderbot hates them. As a thing, Murderbot has never had to deal with anyone looking at him and seeing HIM. It makes him uncomfortable to be looked at because he isn't used to it. He's used to hiding behind his faceplate and his thingness, and there's a freedom in that. It's lonely and demeaning, but also safe. No one has any expectations of him, no one is watching; he can do what he likes. I've never seen a robot/human/what is a person? story where the robot has resisted being treated like a person before. I highly recommend this, maybe even if you don't normally like sci-fi. "It's wrong to think of a construct as half bot, half human. It makes it sound like the halves are discrete, like the bot half should want to obey orders and do its job and the human half should want to protect itself and get the hell out of here. As opposed to the reality, which was that I was one whole confused entity, with no idea what I wanted to do. What I should do. What I needed to do." Murderbot is understandably socially awkward, preferring to watch TV than actually talk to people, and when overstimulated, the poor thing may just walk into a corner to calm down. Wells has captured an adorable awkwardness that is the perfect lens for a scientific adventure out in space. The actual story is fairly simple, with the wrinkle that Murderbot's current crew of humans are scientists who are actually curious how it works. There's bickering, backbiting, and attempts to sneak a killer module into the machine's workings. The whole thing is breezily resolvable once everyone on the mission to be honest with what they've been keeping from each other. You're here for the crew, and you're really here to hear Murderbot's quirky take on the crew and their plight. The real meat is seeing Murderbot stretch their skills, and finding the strength to choose to socialize. From there, they have the opportunity to grow into a person who might escape their existence as a rented weapon of destruction, and venture out into the cosmos in search of a better life and home. My only encounter so far with Martha Wells’ works has been through the first volume of her Tales of the Raksura series, an intriguing combination of fantasy and science fiction that somewhat defies genre definition, and one I intend to return to as soon as I can. I was therefore very curious to read this novella that promised to be quite different, since I enjoy seeing authors flex their proverbial writing muscles in different environments, and I can now say that All Systems Red was a very intriguing experience. On the surface, this novella looks like the deceptively straightforward story of a scientific team exploring an alien world that finds itself threatened by what looks like incorrect information and equipment failure, which is later revealed as an attempt to kill them all to prevent discovery of an unlawful operation. The team is assisted, as required by the Company – the corporate entity supervising every planetary survey – by a SecUnit, an armed and armored android tasked with their protection. This particular SecUnit, though, is different from the other Company-supplied bots, because it’s been able to hack its own governor module, and therefore to act independently from any directive it receives. This mutinous act from the SecUnit, that calls itself Murderbot because of a previous incident, is what defines the whole narrative, taking it away from any predictable path and moving it in unexpected – and sometimes deliciously funny – directions. The story is relayed by Murderbot itself, and as unreliable a narrator as it seems to be, the android speaks in a delightfully cynical voice that sets the tone from the very start, since the SecUnit did not hack its governor module for any dark purpose: all it wants is to be independent from the Company’s nagging presence, with its annoying updates and checks, and be free to enjoy the huge cache of serialized shows it downloaded for its own enjoyment. This is a surprisingly human desire (how many times have we wished to spend a day lounging in front of the tv, instead of having to go to work?), and it sets from the start the parameters for the android’s personality, one that is revealed bit by bit during the course of the story and that manages to make Murderbot a very sympathetic character, one that’s quite easy to root for. If on one side Murderbot is not very fond of humans and tries to avoid their company as much as its duties allow, it does so because of its underlying inability to understand them fully, and in the end its fixation with the serials it’s so fond of might be a way to work toward that understanding through vicarious, less hands-on means. In a way I was reminded of a painfully shy adolescent trying to grasp the finer points of social intercourse by watching tv…. What emerges from the fast-paced narrative is the progressive – and at times even unwilling – change in Murderbot’s psychological profile, which is not so surprising with some hindsight: a bot whose higher aspiration is to be free of superior directives so it can indulge in soap-opera binges is far too human to remain a detached machine for long. Not that our character does not try: we learn soon enough that it feels uncomfortable in the company of humans, that the necessity to lower its visor and show them its face makes it extremely nervous and exposed, which made me wonder how much aware Murderbot is of its difference from the basic SecUnit models, and convinced me of its partial unreliability as a narrator. As the situation gets ever more dangerous for the science team, we see Murderbot change its attitude toward its humans – just as they change their own attitude toward it, accepting it as one of their own with surprising ease – so that it becomes not only their guard but their protector. The desire for freedom of choice, when paired with the need to safeguard the team’s lives (and incidentally its own), morphs into the first inklings of free will, that at first manifests itself in the ability of thinking up a scheme for the group’s survival and later becomes the desire/necessity to explore this amazing changes without further external influence. It’s a fascinating journey from many points of view: because of the construct’s growing self-awareness, of course, but also thanks to Murderbot’s peculiar voice that is an irresistible mix of snark and logical thinking, of innocence (as far as interpersonal relations go) and craftiness. It was a delight following the unit’s journey, and I more than look forward to learning more in the upcoming novellas for this series, which I hope will also expand on the tantalizing details we just glimpsed about this future society. Based on the high reviews and what sounded like a stellar concept, I was expecting to fall in love with this book, but unfortunately it was a disappointment. There's nothing "wrong" with the writing, particularly, or with the story and its characters. Rather, there simply isn't much to either the novella's characters or plot. Throughout the book I couldn't shake the feeling that I was reading only a sliver of a story that needed much more expansion to feel complete. While the book is part of a series, I'm not sure I can forgive the book these flaws, since it never felt fleshed out in its own right. The issue was never that the book wasn't a standalone (in a strange, seemingly contradictory way, it does stand alone), but instead that the narrative simply feels unfinished. If you're looking for a book that deals with artificial intelligence in a meaningful way, with fleshed-out characters and world building, I recommend looking elsewhere. The concept is all over science fiction, and has been executed much more satisfyingly by many more authors. Perhaps, once the series is complete, and it's released in a combined edition it may work better as a story, but the cynical part of me sees this as a simple cash-grab on the part of the publisher (this book is also very expensive considering its length and the quality of the printing, and were one to purchase each of the reported four installments that's upwards of a hundred Canadian dollars for one normal-length book). I don't blame the author at all, rather this read like one in another of a trend of publishing novellas and short stories as "novels" and upping the price for readers. Lots of flash, and attractive to modern readers on the go for its size and length, but lacking in any depth or creativity.

The world development was slim, but you really didn't need any more than the author gave you to understand. The character development was also, just enough. And the pacing, plot, resolution and ending were all equally good. Sometimes the best stories are the ones where you get just enough to understand, connect to, and want more of. I would stop and think to myself sometimes "I wonder what the 'hub" looks like", or "I wonder what color the plants are", but then I realized that I did not need that information, and it would not have necessarily enhanced my reading experience. I am quickly becoming a huge fan of the novella, at least the novellas that are written by authors who can provide you with the full experience without compromising it by keeping it short. I would describe Murderbot as a combination of Breq from Ancillary Justice and Marvin from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy with an unhealthy media addiction. I am interested in learning more about this world too. I was impressed by how real it felt, and how natural the exposition was. We do not learn everything about the world, but everything we learn is something that a person would actually see, think about, or discuss in the situation. All Systems Red is the story of a Security Android assigned to protect a surveying team on a largely uncharted planet. Out of paranoia and boredom he hacks his own governor module and becomes more-or-less autonomous. Free to act out its wildest fantasies. Free to ignore directives from its management system. Protagonist is a security bot -half android and half human, like a cyborg, and from the story it can be inferred that this futuristic society has co-existence of humans, bots and special purpose half bots. Author doesn’t treat this as an existential problem, as the Murderbot itself is content with strict work interactions.
