Martha Wells' "All Systems Red" introduces readers to Murderbot, a security unit that has hacked its governor module to gain autonomy. Despite its newfound freedom, Murderbot prefers to binge-watch media and avoid human interaction. However, it's stuck with a team of scientists on a survey mission on a distant planet. The story is told from Murderbot's cynical and introverted point of view, offering a unique perspective on the interactions between humans and AI. As the team explores the planet, they discover evidence of a previous, failed expedition and soon realize they are not alone. The character development in "All Systems Red" is one of the strongest aspects of the novella. Murderbot is a fascinating and relatable protagonist, despite being an AI construct. Its internal monologue is filled with sarcasm, anxiety, and a surprising amount of empathy. The human characters are also well-drawn, each with their own distinct personalities and motivations. The relationship between Murderbot and the scientists evolves throughout the story, as they gradually come to trust and rely on each other. One of the major plot twists involves the revelation that the previous expedition was deliberately sabotaged, leading to a deadly confrontation with a rival corporation. The tone of "All Systems Red" is a blend of action, humor, and introspection. Wells expertly balances the fast-paced plot with moments of quiet reflection, allowing readers to delve into Murderbot's complex inner world. The novella is filled with witty banter and sarcastic observations, providing plenty of laughs along the way. However, it also explores deeper themes about identity, freedom, and the nature of humanity. Thematically, "All Systems Red" explores the question of what it means to be human, even for a non-human entity. Murderbot's struggle to understand its own emotions and motivations is a central theme of the story. The novella also touches on issues of corporate greed, environmental exploitation, and the ethics of artificial intelligence. Ultimately, "All Systems Red" is a story about finding connection and purpose in a hostile universe. In conclusion, "All Systems Red" is a thrilling and thought-provoking novella that offers a fresh take on the science fiction genre. Martha Wells has created a memorable protagonist in Murderbot, and the story is filled with action, humor, and heart. I don't give many 5-star reviews, because my rating rules set the bar pretty high. This book deserves the top rating; it was both good and fun. And as a novella, it's a useful book-length to use to explore an interesting idea: What is the perspective of an AI (contained in a robot) that is part of a human team in a difficult situation where the AIs training and interests might diverge from the human's? You learn in the first paragraph that the AI should have a constraining governor in it that keeps it from having human-level attachments & feelings, but which is non-functional during the episode of the book. The AI was built to be a killing machine, but forcibly constrained ("covered") to be in the service of humans. When the governor doesn't work, will such an AI be nice to us? This is a question that is "in the air" in popular culture now because of the rapid advancement of AI capabilities and HW/SW. I've heard lots of good things about this one, and I'm happy to say they are all true. (The following facts from the story are not spoilers -- everything I mention below is spelled out within the first few pages.) This is a pretty terrific novella about a biomechanical security-guard type of AI who calls itself Murderbot -- which should tell you right away that it isn't as dispassionately logical or detached as it would like to pretend or as others might see it. In this society this type of AI is treated as a tool, either rented out on contract or sold outright, and nobody pauses to consider that they could be anything more than robots -- but Murderbot has hacked the "governor module" that is supposed to control its behavior, so unbeknownst to anyone it is actually autonomous. It is never made clear (at least in the first installment) just how much (if any) human brain input it actually has (it has a human-appearing head, but we don't know what's inside that head), but Murderbot clearly has emotions -- and social anxiety, which is by turns both funny and touching. Martha Wells is always good with characters, and this one is no exception -- she does a great job of showing instead of telling, and of letting the character grow. I also liked the plot. Murderbot has been rented out on contract to a planetary survey team, and on the new planet things gradually start to go mysteriously wrong. Everyone on the team, including Murderbot, will have to work together, get inventive, and stretch far beyond their comfort zones in order to figure out what's going on, and to survive until rescue can arrive. There's never a dull moment, and though at times the human characters seem too nice to be true, their interactions with Murderbot are great -- and I especially loved how Murderbot's reactions to them changed over time. This novella has been getting a lot of Hugo buzz, and I can see why. I'm certainly going to put it on my nomination ballot. And even the Puppies, if they hadn't already run away from further attempts to manipulate Hugo results, couldn't have much objection to its tone -- sure, there are some Evil People at work, but over all it is really quite optimistic and uplifting in its outlook about both humans and AIs. If you've enjoyed any of Wells's other books, read it. If you enjoy AI-more-human-than-you'd-think stories, read it. I'll certainly be reading the next installment. Must admit, I didn’t know that Martha Wells wrote SF. I do know her Fantasy books (The Cloud Roads, Books of the Raksura), and I thought that her involvement in a SFFWorld ‘Round Table’ forum discussion a few years ago was thoughtful and entertaining, but that for me was about it.* So I was quite pleased when All Systems Red appeared in my review pile. For All Systems is an out and out SF Space Adventure tale, involving AI ‘killerbots’, corporate shenanigans and nasty alien lifeforms on unexplored planets. It’s a great read. “In a corporate-dominated spacefaring future, planetary missions must be approved and supplied by the Company. Exploratory teams are accompanied by Company-supplied security androids, for their own safety. But in a society where contracts are awarded to the lowest bidder, safety isn’t a primary concern. On a distant planet, a team of scientists are conducting surface tests, shadowed by their Company-supplied ‘droid — a self-aware SecUnit that has hacked its own governor module, and refers to itself (though never out loud) as “Murderbot.” Scornful of humans, all it really wants is to be left alone long enough to figure out who it is. But when a neighboring mission goes dark, it's up to the scientists and their Murderbot to get to the truth.” As you can read from the publisher’s blurb, the situation isn’t that different from current writers such as, say, Jay Posey or Ian McDonald – for those of an older persuasion, I’m going to suggest Ben Bova. Where All Systems Red scores though, is that it’s a great set-up – sort’ve like a Science-Fictional version of Dexter. The voice of the AI known as ‘SecUnit’ is great – a knowing, rather sassy but clearly intelligent personality that reminded me of Heinlein’s Mike from The Moon Is A Harsh Mistress or, at times, even Marvin the Paranoid Android from A Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy.  It’s clever and quite depreciating, which appealed to me a lot. “I could have become a mass murderer after I hacked my governor module, but then I realised I could access the combined feed of entertainment channels carried on the company satellites.” Being a novella also means that there’s no space for extraneous waffle. The book begins with a bang, and then rarely lets up. Our Murderbot (the reason for that name is told along the way, but I’ll not spoil it now) is the SecUnit that has to be sent with a survey party by The Company (also later amusingly nicknamed “EvilSurvey”) to explore potential planets for development. In Alien-style plot development, whilst on a planet the team lose contact with the neighbouring survey team from DeltFall, something not too unusual with the cheap and basic equipment hired to them by the Company. However further investigation leads to the discovery of bigger mysteries and the consequences of their discovery. After 144 pages it’s done. And I want more. There are things still unexplained - will the Company find out if the rogue AI is rogue? What is the Company really up to? And what’s the bigger picture? The ending is a bit of a cliffhanger, although I am pleased to type that there will be more in this series. In my opinion, there should be. There’s a pace that meant I read this one near-non-stop, in two sittings. Besides, how often do you read a tale rooting for the bad-guy (who’s clearly not as bad as it makes himself out to be)? Surprisingly good and thoroughly recommended entertainment. * (I now know, from reading the end of this one, that she has also written for the Stargate : Atlantis and Star Wars franchises, which makes sense.)

I thought this was pretty damn good (or, since this is a mass phenomenon, should I say "I agree with the consensus that this is pretty damn good"?). It pulls off an entertaining and moving action sci-fi story in a very streamlined and short package. At the heart of it is the voice of the narrator, a true zeitgeist, spirit of the times, the disembodied voice of a partially embodied era. I will say the facile thing and point out that this book owes a tremendous lot to Mary Shelley, but it's definitely of the now and is a worthy heir. Maybe it's the heir we've been waiting for, finally we get an interminably online So-and-so's Monster to learn about, briefly gasp at, but mostly love. I will avoid diving too much into the nature and mythology of the Murderbot, because I've only just waded into this world and have more to learn. Like all good symbols, the Murderbot is their own, only partially-definable thing and also many things. They're the stand in for the Objectified Human, the homunculus, the Hegelian bondsman, the dehumanized Other. The band of humans in the book are definitely aware of this dynamic and seem motivated to subvert it, motivated by what I read as a mixture of genuine empathy and enlightened savior complex. However, I think what could be interesting about the Murderbot - and I want to read more to find out - is their ability to embody the way men have uniquely been objectified in American culture - as killers, as expendable meat, as having no value outside their labor, as being without feeling - which is something that I have not seen in the spotlight very much in socially-informed literature. I hope it goes somewhere interesting. I also think the Murderbot's voice reflects a kind of antisocial and apathetic personality we currently tend to associate with Gen Z, which is interesting. That is, the avoidance of eye contact, fear of conversations, and complete rejection of industry as a virtue. I don't mean to judge. In many ways, these traits are responsible for making the narrator so relatable. I expect to have more to say about this as I read more of the series. I do think the book is noticeably flawed. The prose can be a little muddy, and I think there are more than a handful of sentences that I think could have been reworked. One could make the argument that this is the narrator, not the author, but I don't experience the mistakes as deliberate. I also think character development was spared for all but a couple of the key players, making the rest of the crew somewhat indistinguishable and difficult to keep track of. But these flaws don't sink the rest of it, and I'm looking forward to reading on. 1 like

Martha Wells’ novella All Systems Red: The Murderbot Diaries is the story of a cybernetic Security Unit that has hacked into its own programming, rendering it capable of autonomous thought and decision-making, although it has most definitely not entertained the notion of letting its employers know about that. It’s designed to be a killing machine, and we see just how good it is at its function in the opening sequence, in which it saves teo human scientists from something large and nasty that attacks them. But what it really enjoys is consuming entertainment media - films, books, music. It’s current contract is to provide security for a group of scientists surveying an uninhabited planet. As contracts go, it’s not a bad one. The scientists are a reasonably compatible group who have worked together before, and after sll, it’s not as if they want to socislise with their SecUnit - and their SecUnit definitely does not want to socialise with them. But after the incident with the large and aggressive lifeform, the SecUnit and the survey team have a serious problem. There’s no mention of the lifeform in the official papers on the planet - and closer inspection shows that those documents have been altered. And that’s just the beginning of the problems. This could have been your standard semi-milsf mystery thriller, and it certainly has all the elements necessary for that, but the unique voice of the narrator transforms it into something rather more interesting, a speculation on the nature of choice, responsibility and autonomy. The self-named “murderbot” has free will, and is not particularly fond of human beings. Yet it risks itself to save its employers, repeatedly. A sense of duty? The need to hide its ability to make decisions, a sort if ironic self-preservation? A sense of right snd wrong? All Systems Red is entertaining as an action-adventure style sf story, but it’s also an interesting turn on the classic AI examination. What is self-awareness? What is free will? What does an autonomous being that has none of the human drives do when it’s left to its own choices? Wells has more stories panned in the Murderbot series planned, and I’ll be interesting in seeing where she takes this. 1 like

June 2018: 4.5 stars Recently, I read Binti by Nnedi Okorafor, which won the 2016 Nebula award for best novella. I was rather underwhelmed by that story. All Systems Red just won the Nebula for best novella for 2018, and I thought that was a much more deserving winner - and a much more engaging and well-written story besides. I think a lot of introverted and nerdy readers on the internet can identify with Murderbot, who has hacked its own governor module and spends all of its downtime (and any other spare moments it can get away with it) consuming the countless hours of entertainment media it has sneakily downloaded. As it points out in the very first lines of the novella, it could have become a mass murdering killing machine after hacking its governor module, but with all that media to consume, who has the time? Murderbot finds social interaction deeply awkward and absolutely hates small talk and especially talking about feelings of any kind, which makes the fact that several of the scientists keep trying to engage it in conversation and treating it as an important member of the crew, not just a mindless droid (it's not mindless, of course, but it also would rather be left alone). Muderbot loves its armour and hates having to be without it, which becomes a bit of an issue as the story goes on - its duty is to protect the scientists and unexpectedly, what was supposed to be a pretty routine research mission turns out to be really rather dangerous. The first instalment of The Murderbot Diaries is an excellent example of why I keep trying science fiction, a genre that is more often than not miss than hit for me. It's not that I hate all sci-fi stories, it's just that the ones that I really like and that manage to really engage me emotionally are few and far between. Since Murderbot clearly is some sort of spiritual cousin to Marvin the Paranoid Android (I first read The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy in my early teens) and also has many of the same anxious reactions to socialising as I frequently do, not to mention wants nothing but to be left alone and consume mindless entertainment, I (like so many other readers) couldn't help but love it. The second novella in this series is out now, but I'm not allowing myself to read it until I'm fully and completely caught up on my backlog. Happily, while it's taking a while, I am slowly but surely churning out reviews and should be able to read about Murderbot's next adventure soon. Murderbot är en säkerhetsenhet som hyrs ut av det stora säkerhetsbolaget. Murderbot, som inte heter Murderbot egentligen, är en construct vilket är en sort cyborg-blandning av robot och klonad människa. Namnet är mer av en arbetsbeskrivning än ett direkt namn. Dess uppdrag är att utföra säkerhetsarbete åt främst undersöknings- och forskarteam på nya planeter. Arbetet består i grunden att försök se till att människorna inte gör så idiotiska saker att de dör. Murderbot har dock hackat det system som ska kontrollera den, vilket gör att den kan tänka själv och ta beslut utanför dess normala säkerhetstänk. Fast mest vill Murderbot bara bli lämnad i fred så att den kan kolla på tv-serier. Men när Murderbot bara gör sitt normala jobb och räddar sina forskare så börjar de plötsligt bry sig om sin säkerhetsenhet och till, Murderbots stora förskräckelse, behandla den som en människa. Jag älskar Murderbot. En cynisk android som inser att den kanske gillar att göra sitt jobb. Om det bara inte var för de där jävla människorna som envisas med att ta de mest korkade beslut möjliga. Murderbot är den mest mänskliga icke-mänskliga SF-karaktären jag läst på länge. Det är omöjligt att läsa dessa böcker och inte älska Murderbot. De båda böckerna är trevligt behändiga kortromaner och ca 150 sidor styck. På dessa sidor lyckas Martha Wells närgånget presentera Murderbot och samtidigt berätta en spännande och tight historia. Artificial Condition är en direkt fortsättning på All Systems Red, men den första boken har ett riktigt slut och om man mot all rimlighet inte skulle vilja läsa visare så känns slutet faktiskt som ett slut. Karaktären Murderbot är mycket underhållande och blir mycket älskvärd i all sin cynism. När den i andra boken dessutom får en ”vän”, ett transportskepp som Murderbot ger namnet ART, vilket är kort för Asshole Research Transport), så blir det ytterligare en mycket underhållande karaktär. Det ska komma ut ytterligare två kortromaner i serien under året och jag har redan förbokat dem. Årets hittills mest underhållande Science fiction!
